stages.title: Advanced literary theory
stages.hook: If the author is "dead" and the reader makes meaning, what is left for criticism to study?
explain: Literary theory asks what literature is, how meaning arises and whose interests texts serve. Structuralism, drawing on Ferdinand de Saussure's linguistics, treats language as a system of signs (signifier and signified) defined by difference. Vladimir Propp's Morphology of the Folktale (1928) found recurring functions in Russian wonder tales, and Gérard Genette developed narratology. Roland Barthes's "The Death of the Author" (1967) argued that a text's unity lies in its reader, not its author.

Post-structuralism questions stable structures: Derrida's différance suggests meaning is endlessly deferred, and Foucault analyses how discourses are tied to power. Marxist critics such as Georg Lukács, Fredric Jameson and Terry Eagleton read texts through ideology and material conditions. Feminist theory, from Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own (1929) to Gilbert and Gubar's The Madwoman in the Attic (1979) and Judith Butler's work on gender performativity, examines gender. Postcolonial theory includes Said, Gayatri Spivak ("Can the Subaltern Speak?", 1988) and Homi Bhabha's hybridity. Mikhail Bakhtin's dialogism and heteroglossia treat novels as many voices in conversation.

Theory is not a single method but a set of questions. Good practice uses theory as a lens, tests it against textual evidence, and is honest about its assumptions. Wimsatt and Beardsley's "intentional fallacy" (1946) warned against settling meaning by authorial intention; the debate continues.

example.q: Classify: "A novel contains many social voices that clash and blend."

stages.limits: Critics dispute whether theory illuminates literature or imposes jargon on it.

stages.title: Historical approaches to literary criticism
stages.hook: Critics have argued about what poetry is for since Plato. How did the questions change over two and a half thousand years?
explain: Western criticism begins with Plato, who in the Republic distrusts poetry as imitation (mimesis) at third remove from truth, and Aristotle's Poetics, which defends tragedy's structure and effect. Horace's Ars Poetica held that poetry should both delight and instruct, and Longinus's On the Sublime asked what produces elevated feeling. Sir Philip Sidney's Defence of Poesy (c. 1580, printed 1595) defended poetry against moral attack, and Samuel Johnson's Preface to Shakespeare (1765) judged the plays by their truth to general nature.

Romantic criticism shifted to imagination and feeling: Wordsworth's Preface to Lyrical Ballads (1800) defined poetry as "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings", and Coleridge's Biographia Literaria (1817) coined the "willing suspension of disbelief". Matthew Arnold made culture a moral project. In the 20th century Russian Formalists such as Viktor Shklovsky stressed defamiliarization, and the New Critics focused on the text.

Non-Western traditions have their own critical histories. Bharata's Sanskrit Natyashastra developed rasa theory, in which art evokes aesthetic flavours such as the heroic and the tender. Liu Xie's Wenxin Diaolong (c. 500) is a major Chinese treatise on literary craft. Arabic and Persian critics analysed rhetoric and poetic imagery. Historical approaches show that criteria of value change with time and power.

stages.title: Comparative global literature
stages.hook: Reading ten thousand novels is impossible. What can we learn about world literature by not reading closely?
explain: Comparative global literature asks how texts circulate and relate across languages. Erich Auerbach's Mimesis (1946), written in exile in Istanbul, traced representations of reality from Homer to the modern novel. Pascale Casanova's The World Republic of Letters (1999) argued that literary value is shaped by an unequal international system with centres such as Paris. David Damrosch emphasises circulation and translation, while Franco Moretti proposed "distant reading", analysing large patterns through data rather than close reading, in works such as Graphs, Maps, Trees (2005).

Critics debate Eurocentrism. Gayatri Spivak's Death of a Discipline (2003) calls for comparison attentive to languages and the planet. Postcolonial and decolonial thought challenges which languages and genres count as literature. Case studies can compare epic, tragedy, the novel and oral forms, asking whether categories like novel travel well: Japan's Tale of Genji, Cervantes and the Chinese Dream of the Red Chamber arise in very different histories.
Good comparative work chooses a clear question, respects each work's language and context, uses translation critically, and avoids both false universals and unbridgeable difference.

example.q: Design: why might distant reading mislead?
steps: It uses data from many texts.
It may miss nuance, language and context.
Therefore it should complement close reading.
example.a: Distant reading complements, not replaces, close reading.

stages.title: Advanced Shakespearean scholarship
stages.hook: If no manuscript in Shakespeare's hand survives of his plays, what exactly do editors edit?
explain: Textual scholarship studies how plays reached print. Some appeared in quartos (single-play editions) in his lifetime, and the First Folio (1623) collected 36 plays. Hamlet exists in a bad quarto (Q1, 1603), a fuller second quarto (Q2, 1604-5) and the Folio text (F1, 1623), which differ in length and wording. Editors choose among them, combine them or print them separately, and these choices affect interpretation.

Authorship scholarship shows Shakespeare collaborated: Pericles with George Wilkins, Timon of Athens and revisions to Macbeth with Thomas Middleton, and Henry VIII and The Two Noble Kinsmen with John Fletcher. Claims that someone else wrote the plays are rejected by almost all scholars, who point to contemporary documentary evidence.

Performance and context studies examine the theatre: the open-air Globe, the indoor Blackfriars, boy actors playing female parts, and the Master of the Revels who licensed plays. Critics such as Jan Kott (Shakespeare Our Contemporary, 1964) read the plays through modern political experience. Global Shakespeare covers translations and adaptations: Sol Plaatje translated Comedy of Errors into Setswana (1930), Julius Nyerere translated Julius Caesar and The Merchant of Venice into Swahili, and Akira Kurosawa's Throne of Blood (1957) reworked Macbeth for Japan.

example.q: Why compare Hamlet Q1, Q2 and F1?
steps: The differences affect what we read.

stages.title: Literary translation and interpretation
stages.hook: If a poem's sound is half its meaning, what exactly are we translating?
explain: Translation is interpretation. Friedrich Schleiermacher (1813) distinguished moving the reader toward the author or the author toward the reader. Lawrence Venuti calls these foreignization and domestication, and in The Translator's Invisibility (1995) criticises fluent translations that hide the translator's work. Eugene Nida distinguished formal equivalence (close to the form of the source) from dynamic equivalence (similar effect on readers). Walter Benjamin's "The Task of the Translator" (1923) treats translation as a means by which a work lives on.

Practical choices include rhyme or no rhyme, register, names, puns and cultural references. Translators choose whether to explain a term in the text, in notes, or leave it. Edward FitzGerald's Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám (1859) was a free, loose English version that became a classic in its own right, while Chapman's Homer inspired Keats. Skopos theory says the purpose of a translation determines its method. Ngũgĩ's practice of self-translation shows how author and translator can be one.

Untranslatability is a debated claim: some terms resist neat equivalents, yet people translate constantly. Machine translation can render information quickly but often struggles with tone, ambiguity and cultural nuance.

example.q: Choose a strategy: translating a Yoruba proverb for English readers.
steps: Foreignizing keeps the original image with a note.
Domesticating replaces it with an English proverb.
example.a: Depends on purpose; each choice has a cost.

analogies.city: Subtitles condense speech to fit a screen.
analogies.tech: Machine translation is fast but literal.

stages.title: Advanced poetry and poetics
stages.hook: Is a poem a verbal object, a speech act, a performance or a piece of music? Poetics gives different answers.
explain: Poetics studies the principles of poetry. Roman Jakobson identified the poetic function of language, which draws attention to the message itself through patterns of sound and structure. T. S. Eliot's "objective correlative" (1919) proposed that emotion in art is expressed through a set of objects or events. John Keats's idea of "negative capability" (1817) valued the capacity to remain in uncertainty.

Prosody studies metre and form: syllabic, accentual and accentual-syllabic verse, free verse, and fixed forms such as the villanelle (19 lines) and sestina (39 lines). The ghazal, from Arabic and Persian poetry, is a series of couplets with a repeated refrain (radif) and rhyme before it (qafia), later flourishing in Urdu. Haiku and tanka are Japanese forms; Kamau Brathwaite's "nation language" brought Caribbean speech rhythms into English poetry.

Poetry exists on the page and in performance. Spoken-word and slam poets draw on oral traditions, as do oral praise poems. Contemporary poetics also considers digital forms and translation. Composition is a craft of revision: reading widely, drafting, cutting, and testing line breaks and sound aloud.

example.q: Identify a form: 19 lines, two repeating refrains.

analogies.home: A refrain in a family song repeats across generations.
analogies.music: The ghazal is sung as well as read.
analogies.tech: Digital poems use code and motion.

stages.mnemonic: Pattern draws attention to the message.
terms: Jakobson's term for language foregrounding its own form.
Eliot's idea of conveying emotion via objects and events.
A poem of couplets with refrain, from Arabic, Persian and Urdu traditions.

misc.wrong: Poetry is just expressing feelings directly.
misc.right: Poets shape feeling through form, image and sound; Eliot argued direct statement is not enough.

stages.limits: Many poets reject fixed definitions of poetry.

stages.title: Global drama and theatrical traditions
stages.hook: Greek tragedy, Noh, Kutiyattam, Alarinjo: does theatre everywhere begin from the same impulse?
explain: Theatre has many origins. Sanskrit drama, theorised in Bharata's Natyashastra, includes rasa and elaborate gesture; Kalidasa's Shakuntala is a classic. Kutiyattam, in Kerala, India, is a Sanskrit theatre tradition performed for centuries. In Japan, Noh developed in the 14th century with Zeami's writings, using masks, ghosts and slow movement; Kabuki emerged in the 17th century. In China, Yuan dynasty zaju includes Guan Hanqing's The Injustice Done to Dou E. Peking opera developed later.

In Africa, Yoruba Alarinjo travelling theatre developed in the Yoruba kingdoms several centuries ago, and Hubert Ogunde developed Yoruba popular theatre in the 20th. Ghana's Concert Party mixed comedy, music and storytelling. Wole Soyinka and Athol Fugard transformed 20th-century drama, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o and Ngũgĩ wa Mirii's community play Ngaahika Ndeenda (1977) was performed by villagers in Gikuyu.

European traditions include Greek and Roman drama, medieval mystery plays, commedia dell'arte and Renaissance theatre. In the 20th century Brecht, Beckett and Augusto Boal's Theatre of the Oppressed (from the 1970s) reimagined performance as a tool for social change. Contemporary theatre travels through festivals, translation and adaptation.

stages.title: Folklore studies and oral literature
stages.hook: Why do folktales about a clever girl and a lost slipper appear from China to Europe?
explain: Folklore studies examines traditional expressive culture: tales, songs, riddles, rituals and beliefs. The Aarne-Thompson-Uther (ATU) index classifies tale types, for example ATU 510A, Cinderella. A Chinese version, Ye Xian, appears in a text from around the 9th century, and many variants exist worldwide. Stith Thompson's Motif-Index catalogues recurring elements. Vladimir Propp's morphology identified narrative functions, while Claude Lévi-Strauss analysed myths as structures of binary oppositions.

Functions: William Bascom proposed that folklore serves education, validation of culture, escape and social control. Performance theory (Richard Bauman, Dan Ben-Amos) treats folklore as communication in context, not just texts. Albert Lord and Milman Parry examined oral composition, Ruth Finnegan oral literature in Africa and Walter Ong "secondary orality".

Ethics and history matter. The Grimms and Elias Lönnrot (Finnish Kalevala) fed national romanticism, collecting and shaping traditions to build identity. Collecting raised questions of ownership, misattribution and appropriation. Today scholars work with communities, respect restricted knowledge and recognise Indigenous cultural and intellectual property. Folklore also lives in new media, memes and urban legends.

example.q: Classify: A mistreated girl, magic help, a lost shoe, a prince.
steps: Ye Xian is an early Chinese variant.

stages.title: Original literary research or creative-writing project
stages.hook: You have a question about a book and a blank page. How do you turn curiosity into an argument or a poem worth reading?
explain: An original literary project is either research or creative, and often both. A research project begins with a focused question, not a topic: not "Shakespeare and women" but "How does Viola's disguise in Twelfth Night shape the play's treatment of desire?" It surveys existing scholarship, states a thesis, defines a method, builds an argument from primary sources (the works) and secondary sources (criticism), and cites everything accurately.

A creative project begins with a purpose and constraints: form, voice, audience, theme. Writers draft freely, then revise by cutting, reordering and testing sound and structure, and seek feedback from readers in workshops. A reflective commentary explains choices of form and influences, connecting creative decisions to literary traditions.

Both require integrity. Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own, and credit is given through citation. Quotations from copyrighted works should be short and attributed; folklore and Indigenous material should be used with consent and credit. Finally, good projects have a clear structure: introduction, development, conclusion, with a revised, edited final form.
